::: {#case .lx-sec}
```{=html}
<div class="lx-case">
<div class="lx-case-part"><p class="lx-eyebrow">1 · The puzzle</p>
<div class="cf4-g"><p class="cf4-gl">The pressure</p><p>Nuclear power supplies reliable low-carbon electricity and high-temperature heat, but existing plants face growing pressure to operate more flexibly in markets with rising renewable penetration.</p></div>
<div class="cf4-g"><p class="cf4-gl">The option</p><div data-e15="E15.2"><p>A nuclear plant can do more than sell electricity around the clock.</p><ul><li>With <span class="lx-term" data-term="high-temperature-electrolyzer">high-temperature electrolysis</span>, part of its electricity and steam can make hydrogen;</li><li>with hydrogen storage and a battery, it can shift its output and offer <span class="lx-term" data-term="ancillary-services">ancillary services</span> to the grid.</li></ul></div></div>
<div class="cf4-g"><p class="cf4-gl">The open question</p><p>Coupling nuclear reactors with hydrogen production through high-temperature electrolysis may improve <span class="lx-term" data-term="flexibility">flexibility</span> and create additional value, yet its economic potential remains uncertain.</p></div>
<p class="lx-hint">So can an existing plant earn more by making hydrogen as well as power?</p></div>
<div class="lx-case-part"><p class="lx-eyebrow">2 · The question in one sentence</p><p class="lx-case-q">Can existing U.S. nuclear power plants improve their economics and operating flexibility by adding high-temperature electrolysis, hydrogen storage and batteries, and by selling energy, hydrogen and ancillary services?</p><p class="lx-hint">Question type: prescriptive (what should be added, and how should it run?).</p></div>
<div class="lx-case-part"><p class="lx-eyebrow">3 · Scale and boundary</p><dl class="lx-ideas cf4-bnd"><dt>Inside</dt><dd data-e15="E15.5"><ul><li>42 operating U.S. reactors in seven <span class="lx-term" data-term="rto">ISO/RTO</span> markets, each facing its own hourly energy and ancillary-service prices for 2024 (8,760 hours; February 29 is left out);</li><li>a high-temperature electrolyzer, hydrogen storage and a battery added to each plant;</li><li>one year of hourly operation turned into a lifetime cash flow.</li></ul></dd><dt>Assumed throughout</dt><dd data-e15="E15.6"><p>a hydrogen production credit of $3/kg for ten years, counted in hydrogen revenue.</p></dd><dt>Left out</dt><dd data-e15="E15.7"><ul><li>price feedback from large-scale adoption, because every plant takes 2024 prices as given;</li><li>re-optimized operation after the hydrogen credit expires, because the dispatch is held fixed.</li></ul></dd></dl></div>
<div class="lx-case-part"><p class="lx-eyebrow">4 · Decisions, goal and rules, in words</p><dl class="cf4-dgr"><div><dt>Decisions</dt><dd data-e15="E15.8"><p>in every hour,</p><ul><li>how much of the plant's electricity and steam goes to the electrolyzer;</li><li>when the electrolyzer runs and at what load;</li><li>what goes into and out of hydrogen storage and the battery;</li><li>grid sales and purchases;</li><li>and the bids of the turbine, electrolyzer and battery in the market's ancillary services.</li></ul></dd></div><div><dt>Goal</dt><dd data-e15="E15.9"><p>the largest yearly profit (energy, hydrogen and ancillary-service revenue minus operating and annualized capital costs), with the hydrogen production credit counted in hydrogen revenue.</p></dd></div><div><dt>Rules</dt><dd data-e15="E15.10"><ul><li>turbine and electrolyzer efficiency follow <span class="lx-term" data-term="piecewise-linear">piecewise-linear</span> curves;</li><li>the electrolyzer keeps <span class="lx-term" data-term="minimum-up-down-time">minimum up and down times</span>, <span class="lx-term" data-term="ramp-rate">ramp limits</span> and a minimum stable load, pays a <span class="lx-term" data-term="start-up-cost">start-up cost</span> and degrades with operation and start-ups;</li><li>ancillary-service bids must fit within each unit's <span class="lx-term" data-term="reserve-headroom">headroom</span> and ramp limits.</li></ul></dd></div></dl></div>
<div class="lx-case-part wide"><p class="lx-eyebrow">5 · Data and method</p><ul><li>Seven U.S. markets price energy and ancillary services differently, and each of 42 reactors faces its own prices.</li><li>The study links an hourly <span class="lx-term" data-term="mixed-integer-program">mixed-integer optimization</span> of turbine, electrolyzer and storage <span class="lx-term" data-term="dispatch">dispatch</span>, for 42 reactors in seven U.S. ISO/RTO markets using 2024 prices, to a lifetime cash-flow model.</li><li>The hourly dispatch model co-optimizes electricity sales, hydrogen production, storage and ancillary services under each market's products, and is run for every reactor.</li></ul>
<details class="lx-deeper cf4-more"><summary><span class="k">Detail</span>What the equipment can do, and the two cases</summary><div class="lx-deeper-body"><ul><li>Electrolyzers and turbines are not ideal: efficiency varies with load, starts wear equipment, and ramping is limited.</li><li>The model represents these limits, so flexibility estimates respect them.</li><li>Each plant is run two ways: business-as-usual operation without any modification for hydrogen production, and a retrofit with high-temperature electrolysis, hydrogen storage and a battery.</li></ul></div></details>
<details class="lx-deeper cf4-more"><summary><span class="k">Detail</span>From one year to a lifetime</summary><div class="lx-deeper-body"><ul><li>The study treats an existing plant's capital as already spent (a <span class="lx-term" data-term="sunk-cost">sunk cost</span>); the retrofit's cash flow adds the capital cost of the new hydrogen and battery equipment.</li><li>A <span class="lx-term" data-term="discounted-cash-flow">discounted cash-flow analysis</span> turns the optimized year into <span class="lx-term" data-term="net-present-value">net present value</span>, <span class="lx-term" data-term="internal-rate-of-return">internal rate of return</span>, <span class="lx-term" data-term="payback-period">payback</span> and levelized costs, with component-level capital costs and scheduled replacements.</li><li>Electricity and hydrogen prices are taken as given (<span class="lx-term" data-term="price-taker">price-taking</span>): the study evaluates plant operation against observed 2024 prices, and price feedback from wide adoption is stated as a limit and left to future work.</li></ul></div></details>
<details class="lx-deeper cf4-more"><summary><span class="k">Detail</span>Sensitivity runs</summary><div class="lx-deeper-body"><p>Sensitivity runs on a representative reactor vary the electrolyzer's capacity bound and the level of electricity prices.</p></div></details></div>
<div class="lx-case-part wide"><p class="lx-eyebrow">6 · What came out, and where it holds</p>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:npph2-existing"><p>Operated as baseload-only plants at 2024 market prices, with no credits, nearly all of the plants studied had negative <span class="lx-term" data-term="net-present-value">net present value</span>.</p><p>With hydrogen integration, including the assumed hydrogen production credit, a majority of the plants studied reached positive net present value.</p><p>With the assumed hydrogen credit, integrated operation added output flexibility: flexible output (the range of a plant's hourly output to the grid) expanded by more than 115 MW for most of the plants studied.</p><p>Ancillary-service revenue was a few percent of total revenue, which includes the hydrogen credit.</p><footer>Approved excerpt of: Li et al. (2026), <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-73630-y">Nature Communications</a>.</footer></blockquote>
<dl class="lx-ideas cf4-holds"><dt>Holds when</dt><dd data-e15="E15.24"><ul><li>2024 prices, taken as given;</li><li>modeled ancillary-service participation parameters;</li><li>the assumed hydrogen credit ($3/kg for ten years), with the dispatch held fixed after the credit expires;</li><li>an existing plant's capital treated as already spent;</li><li>no credits in the baseload case.</li></ul></dd><dt>Leaves out</dt><dd data-e15="E15.24"><p>price feedback from large-scale adoption.</p></dd></dl></div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The toy's day as a small optimization</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

The toy's symbols, for each hour $t$ of the day:

- $p_t$: the grid price, in dollars per MWh sold; $P$: the plant's output, in MW; $E$: the electrolyzer's size, in MW.
- $v = k\,\pi_H$: what a MWh earns as hydrogen, $k$ kg per MWh at an assumed $\pi_H$ dollars per kg.
- $q$: the reserve price, in dollars per MW held for an hour; $c$: the electrolyzer's daily cost, in dollars per MW.
- Decisions: $g_t$ MW to the grid, $h_t$ MW to the electrolyzer, $r_t$ MW held as reserve.

$$\max \; \sum_t \left( p_t\,g_t + v\,h_t + q\,r_t \right) \; - \; c\,E$$

| Rule, in every hour | Why |
|---|---|
| $g_t + h_t = P$ | the plant runs at full power |
| $0 \le h_t \le E$ | the electrolyzer's size |
| $0 \le r_t \le h_t$ | only the electrolyzer's load can be handed back to the grid |
| $g_t \ge P - E \ge 0$ | follows from the first two |

- The best choice: $h_t = E$ when $v + q > p_t$, else $h_t = 0$ (on a tie the toy sells); $r_t = h_t$, or $q = 0$ and $r_t = 0$ with no reserves.
- Against selling all the power, the day changes by $E \sum_t \max(0,\; v + q - p_t) - c\,E$; the plant's own costs appear on both sides, so they cancel.
- Each hour stands alone only because the toy has no storage, start-ups or ramp limits; adding them links the hours into a mixed-integer program, as in [M2](m02-unit-commitment.html) and [M11](m11-tea-in-models.html).

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="cf4-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="sunk" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Whether the electrolyzer pays depends on what the plant itself cost to build.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. That cost is already spent and the same either way, so it drops out: in the toy only the power sold, the hydrogen and reserves earned, and the electrolyzer's own $80,000 a day change.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="headroom" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A plant running at full power can still hold reserves if it runs an electrolyzer.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. Turning the electrolyzer down sends its power to the grid instead, so its load is headroom: in the toy, 200 MW × 20 hours × $8 per MW-hour = $32,000.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-case-try">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Try it yourself</p>
<p class="lx-hint">About 5 minutes, in the toy above.</p>
<p>Start each one from the defaults: press Reset (price level ×1.0, reserve price $8 per MW-hour, electrolyzer 200 MW, reserves offered).</p>
<ul>
<li>Set the price level to ×0.6, then to ×1.4. In how many hours does the electrolyzer run, and how does the day compare with selling all the power?</li>
<li>Turn reserves off. In how many hours does the electrolyzer run now, and how much of the day's gain came from reserves?</li>
<li>Set the electrolyzer to 0 MW, then to 400 MW. What range of output to the grid does each give, and what happens to its cost?</li>
<li>Pick 13:00, then 19:00 on a chart. Where does each MWh go, and why?</li>
</ul>
<!-- cf4-worked:start (written by the test's --write mode from the data and the model; do not edit) -->
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Worked answers, each from the toy's defaults</summary><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Setting, from the defaults</th><th scope="col">Result, against selling all the power</th><th scope="col">Why</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Price level ×0.6</th><td class="n">runs in all 24 hours; $91,240 better</td><td class="n">The dearest hour pays $54 per MWh, less than the $58 a MWh earns as hydrogen and reserve. $171,240 gained before its cost, minus its $80,000.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Price level ×1.4</th><td class="n">runs in 16 of 24 hours; $8,360 worse</td><td class="n">In 8 hours the grid pays more than $58 per MWh. $71,640 gained before its cost, minus its $80,000.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Reserves off</th><td class="n">runs in 19 hours, not 20; $2,200 better, not $33,400</td><td class="n">At 17:00 the grid's $54 per MWh beats $50 as hydrogen alone. Reserves were 3.2% of revenue, yet the gain falls by $31,200.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Electrolyzer 0 MW</th><td class="n">output to the grid 1,000 MW all day; no different</td><td class="n">Nothing goes to hydrogen, and there is no electrolyzer to pay for.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Electrolyzer 400 MW</th><td class="n">output to the grid 600 to 1,000 MW; $66,800 better</td><td class="n">It runs in the same 20 hours. $226,800 gained before its cost, minus its $160,000.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Pick 13:00</th><td class="n">200 MW to the electrolyzer, 800 MW to the grid</td><td class="n">The grid pays $12 per MWh, less than the $58 a MWh earns as hydrogen and reserve.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Pick 19:00</th><td class="n">all 1,000 MW sold</td><td class="n">The grid pays $90 per MWh, more than the $58 a MWh earns as hydrogen and reserve.</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>The plant's own costs are the same in every case, so they never enter.</p></details>
<!-- cf4-worked:end -->
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-case-try">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">With open code</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Optional, about 30 minutes; needs Python 3.10 or later on your computer (<a href="b02-python-data.html">lesson B2</a>).</p>
<p>Try it yourself: the framework's minimal example compares business as usual with the integrated system over two synthetic weeks, solved with HiGHS.</p>
<p>Generate synthetic inputs, then run the hourly operation again with energy prices 15% higher, or with ancillary services in dispatch mode, and compare the revenues and the flexibility.</p>
<p>Its numbers say nothing about any real plant, market, policy or year.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Set it up first: clone the repository and install it as its README's <a href="https://github.com/Henryutd2021/nuclear-hydrogen-integration#quick-start">Quick start</a> says; run the commands in the repository's folder.</p>
<ul class="cf4-cmds"><li><code>python examples/minimal.py</code></li><li><code>nuclear-h2 synthetic my_inputs/ --storage</code></li><li><code>nuclear-h2 run my_inputs/ --out-dir outputs/base</code></li><li><code>nuclear-h2 run my_inputs/ --price-factor 1.15 --out-dir outputs/price_up</code></li><li><code>nuclear-h2 run my_inputs/ --as-mode dispatch --out-dir outputs/dispatch</code></li></ul>
<p class="lx-hint">Each run writes <code>revenue_musd_per_yr.csv</code> and <code>summary.json</code> into its <code>--out-dir</code> folder. Compare the revenue tables, and <code>grid_output_range_mw</code> under "flexibility" in <code>summary.json</code>: the range of output to the grid, the toy's measure too.</p>
<p><a href="https://github.com/Henryutd2021/nuclear-hydrogen-integration">nuclear-hydrogen-integration</a>: open code · MIT licence.</p>
</div>
```
